extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning to practise literary/poem criticism; aspiring critics and teachers of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for reading and judging lyric poems, focusing on metre, diction, imagery, sincerity, and reader-responses. Emphasises close reading and distinguishing poem-internal qualities from readers' prejudices or stock reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem's metre should fit and express its content; form and movement must match the thought so that rhythm aids understanding rather than misleads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and warnings throughout: 'The metre is regular...' and 'the form fits the contents to perfection.' Beware of a 'dangerous metre to use unless the poetic thought is really fine' — an unsuitable metre can cause readers to 'go thudding away' and miss the poem's meaning. Note cases where the rhythm 'seems to leap forward' to keep pace with thought; readers who impose external canons of metrical regularity may fail to apprehend intended contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity / lucidity of sense
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should be sufficiently clear that readers can grasp what the author means without undue obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers praised the poem for being 'clearer and more easy to understand.' Collocation of poems can influence perception of clarity; mutual influence between pieces presented together may mislead. Clarity does not preclude depth—meaning may not be exhausted on first reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmosphere and mood suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem should establish and sustain an atmosphere appropriate to its theme (e.g., a prayerful atmosphere for devotional material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes an 'atmosphere of the poem is that of a prayer' and that metre and rhythm contribute to a 'general impression of quiet orderliness' suited to the theme. Evaluate whether sound and diction evoke the claimed atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / authenticity of motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the shaping impulse of the poem is genuinely the feeling it professes (distinguishing crude insincerity from subtler self-deception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish crude, deliberate insincerity from subtler forms where the writer cannot distinguish genuine promptings from those he would like to have. Signs of compromised imaginative integrity include exaggeration, strained expression, false simplicity, and indebtedness to other poetry. Richards notes the difficulty of proving sincerity from a single poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of expression and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Word choice and phrasing should be apt, natural to the thought, and not strained, forced, or incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous examples: complaints about 'so meet a place,' 'Haply ... may work in me,' 'poised feet,' 'boom of the tingling strings' and confusions between 'tingling' and 'tinkling.' 'Unpoetical' words can be defensible if they serve the incident. Watch for forced diction that produces ludicrous or homiletic effects; also note when 'perfect communication' is achieved by simple, appropriate language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of pathetic fallacy / over-anthropomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious attributing human feelings or worship to natural objects (e.g., 'the trees worship'); check whether such attributions are metaphoric, overworked, or functioning as argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics raised the 'pathetic fallacies' objection: 'The trees don't worship, arise, or run.' Determine whether attribution is used as mere ornament or as an argumentative device; if overworked it becomes a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and single-idea focus
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful poem often confines itself to one central idea or unifying motif, with each part contributing to that unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praised as 'Simplicity and unity seem to me the outstanding qualities... There is only one central idea: the bond between man and nature in mutual worship.' Consider whether verses admit extraneous trains of thought or maintain strict conformity to the central idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery aptness and risk of unintended literalness
rubrics_metrics.description: Images must be apt and not produce unintended, ludicrous literal pictures that undercut tone or purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the third verse evoking an image of a forward breaking away 'with never a swerve' that suggested a rugby run; such literal misreadings can make an image seem ridiculous. 'The precise image let loose cannot of course be counted against the poet; the tendency towards the exaggerated and ludicrous might.' Check whether vivid images echo elsewhere and indicate a tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: avoid smugness and self-conscious grand manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone should not be self-satisfied, sententious, or commercialised; grand manner that feels contrived repels readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many criticisms focus on 'smugness', 'sententious egoism', 'stark Grand Manner... over-studied and over-stated.' Verse that appears 'prim' or 'mercenary' suggests loss of spontaneity; homiletic or domestic sermonizing ('Parable is served up cold') is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs stock/responsive triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the poem's appeal is intrinsic or due to ready-made stock responses and familiar associations external to the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The revival of 'a set of feelings very ready to be revived' or frequent references to stock images ('forest-aisles') can explain popularity without proving literary merit. Be alert to 'stock responses' that come from readers' prior training rather than the text itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close reading of details and contrasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful attention to word differences, contrasts, and fine details is essential; superficial or summary readings miss vital clues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: failure to distinguish 'tingling' from 'tinkling' or to work out contrast between 'great black piano' and parlour instrument leads to misreading. Richards emphasises comparing comments with closeness of reading; close reading uncovers intended contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aptness and coherence of metaphor and figurative language
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors must be coherent with the poem's world; if a metaphor would be literally false in the poem's implied context, it risks being valueless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted: 'If the fourth verse is not literally true, the metaphor is valueless. If it is true, the trees should not be in a lyric of faith, but in a Botanic Garden.' Evaluate metaphors alongside related diction for echoes that reveal tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional restraint: avoid mawkish sentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem should not wallow in facile, trivial emotion or rely on 'appeals to the gallery'; sincerity of emotion must be matched by artistry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics called passages 'silly, maudlin, sentimental twaddle' and warned against 'revelling in emotion for its own sake.' Check versification and whether emotion is supported by craft instead of mere sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish poem-internal effects from reader projection
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a reader's response reflects the poem itself or the reader's own private poem, associations, or prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many responses 'wander off' into personal reminiscence; Richards warns that 'most of the admirers were more occupied by the effect of the poem on their feelings than by the detail of the poem itself.' Criticism should seek evidence that reactions are grounded in the text, not external reminiscence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider cumulative evidence: single faults vs tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: A single awkward word or line may be mere clumsiness, but repeated echoes can indicate a persistent tendency in diction or thought that is significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richard's method: a single fault 'taken by itself, becomes evidence of a tendency when it finds echoes.' To judge whether a flaw is isolated or symptomatic, consider other diction items like 'so meet a place,' 'central fire,' 'fill' and 'sacramental' appearing elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rhythm to express progression of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythmic changes should mirror the movement of thought or emotion (e.g., a leap forward in rhythm to match an emotional surge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: 'The two first lines of the third verse perfectly express the meaning by their sudden change of rhythm.' Assess whether rhythmic shifts successfully convey progression or are merely accidental.
